general_guidance: Loss of appetite in cattle or buffalo can have many causes including fever, digestive issues (bloat, impaction), respiratory infections, or pain. Check the animal's temperature (normal: 38–39°C). Ensure fresh water is available. Observe for other signs like bloating, diarrhea, nasal discharge, or labored breathing. Mild loss of appetite for less than 24 hours in an otherwise alert animal may be monitored. Offer palatable green fodder. Do NOT force-feed.
red_flags: complete refusal for more than 24 hours
limitations: Loss of appetite is a non-specific symptom. This guidance cannot determine the underlying cause. A veterinarian must examine the animal to diagnose correctly.
source_name: NDDB (National Dairy Development Board) — Animal Health Guidelines

general_guidance: Bloat (tympany) can be life-threatening. Contact a qualified veterinarian immediately, especially if the abdomen is rapidly enlarging or breathing is difficult. Keep the animal calm and do not force-feed, give oils or other home remedies, or attempt to insert a tube. Follow the veterinarian's instructions while arranging urgent care.
red_flags: animal has been bloated more than 30 minutes and worsening
limitations: Bloat can become life-threatening quickly. This information is not a diagnosis or treatment; a qualified veterinarian must assess the animal urgently.
source_name: ICAR — Indian Council of Agricultural Research, Livestock Health Guidelines

general_guidance: Normal temperature of cattle and buffalo is 38–39°C (100.4–102.2°F). A temperature above 39.5°C is considered fever. Fever is usually a sign of infection (bacterial, viral, or parasitic). Keep the animal in a cool, shaded area. Provide fresh clean water. Do NOT give human medicines like paracetamol — cattle doses are very different and potentially dangerous. Only a licensed veterinarian should prescribe antipyretics or antibiotics.
red_flags: sudden high fever with multiple animals affected (suggests contagious disease)
limitations: Fever is a symptom, not a disease. Without examination and diagnostic tests, the cause cannot be determined. Administering medicines without veterinary guidance can mask symptoms and delay proper treatment.

general_guidance: Diarrhea in cattle can be caused by diet changes, parasites, or bacterial/viral infection. Provide clean fresh water to prevent dehydration — this is the most important first aid. Oral Rehydration Solution (ORS) can be given: mix 1 teaspoon salt + 1 teaspoon sugar in 1 litre water. Withhold concentrate feed temporarily. Offer dry hay/straw. Monitor for blood in stool (serious sign).
red_flags: severe dehydration (sunken eyes, skin doesn't spring back)
limitations: Diarrhea has many possible causes. ORS is supportive care only. Antibiotics and anthelmintics should only be prescribed by a veterinarian after proper diagnosis.

general_guidance: Reduced milk production can be due to mastitis (udder infection), nutritional deficiency, heat stress, illness, pregnancy, or natural decline at end of lactation. Check udder for swelling, hardness, redness, or pain (signs of mastitis). Check for watery or stringy milk — a sign of mastitis. Ensure adequate water intake (a lactating cow needs 50–80 litres/day). Maintain a balanced diet with green fodder.
red_flags: animal refusing milking due to pain
sudden drop in all animals (suggests contagious mastitis)
limitations: Mastitis requires veterinary diagnosis and appropriate antibiotic treatment prescribed by a vet. Self-medication with antibiotics causes antibiotic resistance and affects milk safety.

general_guidance: For external wounds: clean the wound gently with clean water or saline. Remove visible dirt or foreign material carefully. Apply antiseptic solution (povidone-iodine / betadine, diluted) if available. Cover with clean cloth to protect from flies. Do NOT apply turmeric, ash, dung, or other traditional substances to open wounds — these can cause serious infections. For fly-strike (maggots in wound): remove maggots carefully with tweezers or turpentine oil on a cotton swab, clean thoroughly, and seek veterinary care.
red_flags: uncontrolled bleeding (press firmly with clean cloth and call vet immediately)
signs of tetanus (jaw stiffness, muscle spasms)
limitations: Deep wounds, puncture wounds, and bite wounds carry serious infection risks including tetanus and gas gangrene. A veterinarian should assess all significant wounds.
source_name: ICAR — First Aid for Farm Animals

general_guidance: Buffalo and cattle suffer significantly in high temperatures (above 35°C). Signs: rapid panting, excessive salivation, reluctance to move, reduced feed intake, milk drop. First aid: move animal to shade immediately. Provide plenty of fresh cool water. Sprinkle cool (not ice cold) water on the body, especially neck and flanks. Improve ventilation. Do NOT give ice water to drink — can cause shock. Schedule work and milking for early morning or evening.
red_flags: animal collapsed or unable to stand due to heat
limitations: Severe heat stroke in animals can be fatal. If the animal shows collapse or very high temperature, veterinary emergency care is needed immediately.
source_name: ICAR — Heat Stress Management in Dairy Animals

general_guidance: A cow or buffalo that cannot stand is a SERIOUS EMERGENCY. This could indicate: Milk Fever (Hypocalcaemia — very common in dairy cows after calving), Grass Tetany (Hypomagnesaemia), severe injury, nerve damage, or severe illness. Do NOT attempt to force the animal to stand — this can cause further injury. Keep the animal in sternal position (on its chest, not its side). Prevent bloat. Contact a veterinarian IMMEDIATELY — milk fever can be fatal within hours but responds rapidly to calcium injection.
red_flags: animal down for more than 1 hour
limitations: A downed animal cannot be safely treated at home. Calcium and magnesium injections must be administered by a trained veterinarian. Delay significantly worsens prognosis.
source_name: ICAR — Metabolic Disorders in Dairy Cattle

general_guidance: Coughing and nasal discharge in goats/sheep often indicate respiratory infection (Pneumonia, Contagious Caprine Pleuropneumonia - CCPP, or Peste des Petits Ruminants - PPR). Isolate the affected animal from others immediately. Keep in a dry, well-ventilated but draft-free area. Provide clean fresh water. Check for fever. PPR is a highly contagious viral disease — if multiple animals are affected with fever, nasal discharge, diarrhea, and mouth sores, contact a government veterinarian immediately as it is a notifiable disease.
red_flags: mouth sores with nasal discharge (PPR suspected)
limitations: Respiratory disease in small ruminants can spread rapidly and some diseases (PPR) are notifiable. Self-medication with antibiotics without diagnosis is dangerous. PPR requires vaccination — contact local animal husbandry department.
source_name: ICAR — Health Management in Goats and Sheep

general_guidance: Diarrhea in goats and sheep is very common and a major cause of death in kids/lambs. Common causes: internal parasites (worms — very serious in small ruminants), coccidiosis, enterotoxaemia, or diet change. Provide ORS (Oral Rehydration Solution) to prevent dehydration. Keep the animal warm and dry. BOTTLE LAMBS AND KIDS: seek veterinary care within hours of severe diarrhea. Internal parasites (Haemonchus contortus — barber's pole worm) are a leading killer of goats — regular deworming schedule should be planned with a vet. Check 'FAMACHA' lower eyelid color — pale/white suggests severe anaemia from worms (emergency).
red_flags: very pale or white lower eyelid (FAMACHA score 4-5)
kid or lamb with severe diarrhea
limitations: Parasite resistance to dewormers (anthelmintic resistance) is a serious problem. Dewormer selection and dosing must be guided by a veterinarian. Do not worm routinely without veterinary advice.

general_guidance: Normal goat/sheep delivery (kidding/lambing) should complete within 30 minutes of active straining. If the animal has been straining for more than 30 minutes without delivery, this is a VETERINARY EMERGENCY (Dystocia). Signs of normal delivery: water bag appears, then feet and head. Do NOT attempt to pull a stuck kid/lamb without veterinary training — incorrect traction can injure or kill the mother and offspring. Retained placenta (jhari/jer nahi giri): if placenta is not expelled within 12 hours, contact a veterinarian.
red_flags: straining more than 30 minutes without delivery
visible feet but no progress for 15 minutes
only one foot or abnormal presentation visible
limitations: Assisted delivery requires veterinary training. Incorrect intervention is dangerous. Time is critical in dystocia — call a veterinarian immediately do not delay.
source_name: ICAR — Reproductive Health in Small Ruminants

general_guidance: Suspected poisoning in any animal is a VETERINARY EMERGENCY. Signs: sudden collapse, convulsions, excessive salivation/frothing, muscle tremors, dilated pupils, difficulty breathing. Do NOT try to induce vomiting in ruminants. Remove the animal from the suspected poison source. Contact a veterinarian or nearest veterinary hospital IMMEDIATELY. Try to identify and save a sample of what the animal may have eaten.
limitations: Poisoning treatment requires specific antidotes and supportive care that only a veterinarian can provide. Every minute counts. Do not delay.

general_guidance: Vaccination is the most effective way to prevent serious livestock diseases. Key vaccines in India: (1) FMD (Foot and Mouth Disease / Khur-Muh Rog): Cattle and buffalo — every 6 months. Free government vaccination drives are conducted. (2) HS (Haemorrhagic Septicaemia): Cattle and buffalo — annually before monsoon. (3) BQ (Black Quarter): Cattle — annually. (4) PPR (Peste des Petits Ruminants): Goats and sheep — every 3 years. Contact your local Pashu Chikitsa Kendra (Veterinary Centre) or Animal Husbandry Department for free vaccination schedules.
limitations: Vaccination schedules may vary by region. Contact your local animal husbandry department for the current schedule and free vaccination camps in your area.
source_name: Department of Animal Husbandry & Dairying, Government of India

general_guidance: Eye problems (Infectious Bovine Keratoconjunctivitis — Pinkeye — or Pink Eye) are common in cattle, especially young stock. Signs: watery eye, keeping eye closed, cloudiness, redness. Gently clean discharge with clean damp cloth. Keep animal in shade — bright sunlight worsens condition. Flies spread the infection — fly control is important. Isolate the affected animal to prevent spread. Eye drops should only be used as prescribed by a veterinarian.
red_flags: complete white cloudiness of the eye (corneal ulcer)
limitations: Some eye conditions can cause permanent blindness if untreated. Veterinary examination is recommended for any eye problem lasting more than 2 days.

general_guidance: Ticks (Chichad) and lice are very common external parasites that cause significant production losses, anaemia, and transmit diseases. Regular grooming helps detect them early. Chemical acaricides (tick/lice killers) are available — consult your veterinarian for appropriate product and safe application, especially near eyes and genitals. Tick control in the environment (sheds) is also important. Manual removal of individual ticks: grasp close to skin and pull steadily — do NOT crush.
red_flags: severe tick burden causing anaemia (pale gums)
skin disease/mange with large areas of hair loss
limitations: Some tick-borne diseases (Theileriosis, Babesiosis) can be life-threatening. If the animal shows signs of anaemia, fever, or jaundice along with tick infestation, contact a veterinarian urgently.

general_guidance: Lameness is common in livestock and can be caused by hoof overgrowth, foot rot (bacterial infection between toes), injury, or FMD (Foot and Mouth Disease — with lesions in mouth too). Check for: interdigital (between toes) swelling or foul smell (foot rot). Clean and trim overgrown hooves. For foot rot: clean affected foot thoroughly, apply antiseptic (povidone-iodine). Foot rot requires veterinary treatment with antibiotics. FMD: contact government veterinarian immediately — it is a highly contagious notifiable disease.
red_flags: foot lesions with mouth sores (FMD suspected)
severe lameness with swelling extending above the hoof
limitations: FMD is a notifiable disease and must be reported to the animal husbandry department. Severe foot rot requires prescription antibiotics from a veterinarian.
source_name: NDDB — Hoof Health in Dairy Animals

general_guidance: After normal calving: (1) Ensure the calf breathes — clear mucus from nose and mouth. (2) The calf MUST receive Colostrum (first milk / Kheesra) within the first hour — this provides critical immunity. Minimum: 2 litres within first 2 hours, 2 more litres within 6 hours. (3) Check that the placenta passes within 12 hours. (4) Check the calf is standing within 1-2 hours and nursing. (5) Mother: provide warm water with jaggery (gur) and salt, green fodder. Do NOT milk the cow completely for the first few days — let the calf feed first.
red_flags: calf not breathing after birth (clear airway, rub body vigorously)
limitations: If the calf appears weak or is not nursing, veterinary support within hours is critical. Failure to receive colostrum significantly increases mortality risk.

general_guidance: Internal parasites (roundworms, tapeworms, liver flukes) are a major cause of production loss and death in Indian livestock. Signs: weight loss despite eating, pot belly (especially kids/lambs), pale gums, poor coat condition, diarrhea. A proper deworming schedule should be established with a veterinarian. Importantly: do NOT give the same dewormer every time — rotate between drug classes to prevent resistance. Kids and lambs need more frequent deworming. After deworming, pasture management also helps break the parasite cycle.
red_flags: very pale gums (white) — severe anaemia from worm burden
multiple sudden deaths in young animals
limitations: Anthelmintic (dewormer) resistance is a serious and growing problem in India. A veterinarian should guide dewormer selection and monitor effectiveness. Random deworming without diagnosis wastes money and accelerates resistance.
source_name: ICAR — Parasitic Diseases of Small Ruminants

general_guidance: Labored or rapid breathing in livestock is always serious. Causes include pneumonia, heat stress, bloat pressing on lungs, heart disease, or anemia. Count breaths per minute (normal cattle: 10-30/min; goats/sheep: 12-20/min). More than 50 breaths per minute is concerning. Keep animal calm and in a cool, well-ventilated area. Remove from direct sun. Contact a veterinarian promptly.
red_flags: neck extended and head raised trying to breathe
limitations: Severe respiratory distress is a medical emergency. Time is critical. Do not delay seeking veterinary care to try home remedies.
